The House in committee of Supply, Mr. Gordon in the chair:
Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment-capital, 510,000.

Will the minister explain
this vote?

speakeroldname: Hon. H. S. BELAND (Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment):
speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: It is used for the replacement of equipment and the purchase of small fixtures. The largest items for replacement of equipment are attended to by the Department of Public Works. This vote covers a very large number of small articles which have been broken or rendered useless. The list is extremely long, probably over a thousand articles are covered by it; ranging from sixty cents to around one hundred dollars. The largest outlay, $1,076.50, was to provide an X-ray equipment for the Christie street hospital Toronto.
What was the total used last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: It was $7,416.

Mr. Chairman, when the estimates of this department were before the 270
House at a late hour some weeks ago, I was not present, and I notice that the minister made certain references to some remarks of mine when I spoke on the budget. I should like to acknowledge the courtesy with which he referred to my remarks, differing as he did so entirely from my criticism. He was also good enough to say that he had no doubt that I did not wish to mislead the House. That, Mr. Chairman, is most assuredly the case. I should like, therefore, to go a little further into the matter and describe the basis on which I built my criticism.
My criticism is that this department has outlived its usefulness, and that considerable economies could be effected were it abolished. The raison d'etre for the creation of this department was to give assistance to the unfit men with the object of helping them in their return to civil life, and it does not appear to me that an examination of the expenses incurred by the department should be confused by the inclusion of expenses connected with pensions. I notice on turning to the Auditor General's reports that the amount included for this department is between $10,000,000 and $10,500,000. There are one or two sums comparatively small-where we are speaking of millions-included in that amount which for the purposes of my argument, I deduct, as the cost of the federal appeal board, $82,715, Public Service Retirement Act, $1,120, salaries and contingencies of the Board of Pension Commissioners, $97,523. After making these deductions I arrive at a total of $10,230,149. That I divide into three categories: salaries, $4,711,549; administration, which covers various payments made on behalf of the unfit men. such as care of patients, vocational expenses, operating expenses and the like, $2.793,541; and payments to the unfit men, $2,725,059.
At that point I make a further adjustment for the reasons I have given, in that I do not consider that the expenses connected with pensions should be included in this investigation. I consider it only fair that we should deduct those expenses. The minister has said that he does not know what they amount to, and that it would be an intricate piece of accountancy to ascertain their total. So I think we must make an approximation of the amount. In the year prior to the amalgamation we know that such expenses amounted to a little over a million and a quarter. I do not think it can be contended that they have increased since that date, it is more probable that they have somewhat decreased, for there have been fewer boards, less travelling, and

Supply-Re-establishment

presumably an increase of efficiency in the routine work. I suggest then, that instead of a million and a quarter dollars, it would be reasonable to make a reduction of $900,000 for those expenses. A portion of that wmuld come under the head of salaries, another portion under the head of payments made for the men. I therefore deduct $500,000 from salaries and the balance, $400,000, from the administrative charges.
Now, the minister takes issue with me for putting all the expenditures, other than the payments to the men, into one category, for I have shown that those payments to the returned men have dropped from 56 per cent in 1920 to 29 per cent in 1924. But had I dissected these percentage figures then as I propose to do now, it would not injure my argument and I do not think it would help the minister, for it will be seen that over the course of the five years those administrative charges have remained just about constant; they varied from 23 per cent of the total in 1920 to 26 per cent in 1924. It follows then that if the payments to the men have dropped and the administrative charges have remained constant, the percentage of salaries must have increased, and they have so increased from 20 per cent in 1920 to 45 per cent in 1924.
The controversy then turns on whether it is a reasonable thing to take out the expenditures for pensions from this set of figures in order to analyse the cost to the department. I think it is, but in that the minister and I do not agree. These costs had been dealt with separately before the amalgamation, and I do not think we should becloud the issue by including them in examining into the percentage costs of the department. The pension costs can certainly not have advanced since the amalgamation, . and I contend that if the government had been thrilled with a desire to economize in all direction!?, very considerable economies could have been effected in this department.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
My hon. friend does not
seem to repent of the broad and, as I consider it, unwarranted statement he made on a previous occasion. He refuses to take into consideration the administration of pensions; why he should take this attitude, I do not know. The administration of pensions is a very important activity of the department, relating, as it does, to the payment of small amounts monthly to pensioners and dependents of pensioners. A close check has to be kept upon all amounts paid out and upon all the transactions in connection with the making,
[Mr Stirling.]
repealing or altering of awards, births in the family of a pensioner, remarriages of widows, and so on. My hon. friend a moment ago, in what I am pleased to consider a well meant argument, stated that the administration of pensions at this day should be easier, less' complicated or less involved than it was in 1916, 1917, 1918 and 1919. Well, I beg to disagree with him. I think I would be supported Iby medical men generally in the contention that the further we get from the war the more difficult it becomes to diagnose a case. Claims for pension or increases in pension have been almost innumerable during the last five years, and it stands to reason that the work of the medical officer is all the more difficult as we get further away from the time when the disability was actually incurred. If my hon. friend is fair I am sure he will agree with me in this regard. We are confronted with great difficulty when it comes to determining claims for pension at this time on account of war disability. The work, therefore, is more complicated, more involved, more difficult to-day than it was at that time. My hon. friend quoted a certain figure as representing the direct handing of money from the department to the men-what he is pleased to call cash payments. I do not agree with him on the figure, in the first place. Even leaving aside the pensions, which are paid direct to the pensioner, and which amount to a good deal more than he seems to contend, has my hon. friend taken into consideration the payment of claims under the insurance scheme?

I have included the
following in the third category: Pay and allowance, vocational loans, interest on war service gratuity, unemployment relief, employers' liability compensation, recommendations of Pensions committee, repatriation, and compensation for death or injury re flying.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Whoever	prepared that
statement for my hon. friend must have done so with the idea of making a case. Why did my hon. friend's informant not include insurance payments? [DOT]

Where	is that included
in the Auditor General's report?

speechtext:
I do not know whether

Now, in this connection there has been a misrepresentation of the facts. My hon. friend says that services rendered to the men cannot be considered as cash payments.

Supply-Re-establishment
Strictly speaking we can agree upon that. But if my hon. friend was taken ill on the road in front of my house and I invited him to come in and occupy a room in my house for two months; and if I had my physician administer treatment to him, and furnished him with food during that period, would he not consider, in the absence of any cash payment, that what he had received from me was equivalent to cash?

Certainly I would. I
would put it in the category of those payments which have remained constant during the period we are discussing.

speechtext: What is the amount under that category?

I will quote the amounts
paid out in the various services:

With other minor items, this makes a total of $5,648,188.40. With all due deference to my hon. friend I contend that these services are absolutely equivalent to money paid to the men. Not a cent of it goes for administration purposes. True, the money is paid in salaries; but does my hon. friend think that because public money is paid to the postmaster in his town or city for the service of receiving and delivering mail the public does not get the benefit of it? This I think illustrates my contention. Thousands of postmasters throughout the country render a definite service to hon. gentlemen in this House as well as to other citizens of the country. But does any of the money which is paid to them in the way of salaries reach the public? Not at all. Yet the public benefits directly from that service. The principle is the same in 270i	[DOT]
this case. The man who is treated in hospital, who receives the attendance of a doctor paid by the state, the attendance of a nurse also paid by the state; the man who receives drugs which are necessary in his case and which are paid for with public money; the man who receives from the hospital food which is provided by the same means, is benefiting directly although he gets no money. It is all very well to say, "You have paid the money in salaries to nurses, physicians, orderlies, laundry people and power plant men, and your expenditure is therefore made uj) largely of such disbursements." Well, I admit that it is made up largely of salaries. But you cannot dispense with the services of those to whom these salaries are paid. Let me ask my hon. friend in all sincerity, if he were in my place would he stop any of these services? He would not.

Is the minister referring
to items paid to the hospitals for care of patients as items which I have considered in the category of salaries?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
What is the amount paid
out in salaries for administration and other purposes as given in the report?

The salaries amount to
$4,711,000 odd.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
These amounts are paid
in salaries for services rendered to the men, and without those services the work could not possibly be carried on.
Why does the amount of salaries go on increasing year by year in proportion to the total?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
The amount paid in
salaries is not increasing; it is decreasing year by year in relation to the total paid out annually. If you paid $24,000,000 five years ago in pensions and to-day you pay $34,000,000 it is obvious that more iwork is entailed. Indeed, the work is a great deal more difficult now than it was at that time. And the amount paid in salaries, as well as the number of medical men employed, is being reduced.

I am not contending
that it is not. The amounts paid in salaries have decreased but the percentage on the total has increased.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I do not admit that for
a moment. The number of employees for administrative purposes has substantially decreased. It 'has been painful in many instances to make the reductions as rapidly as we have done, because one must bear in mind that the great majority of the men employed
Supply-Re-establishment

in the department are returned men, many of whom, although I do not know exactly what proportion, are disabled.
Both under the late administration and under this government the number has been reduced by something like seven or eight hundred a year, and during the last thirteen months we have decreased the staff of the department by five hundred. On April 1, 1924, we had 2,922 employees and on May 1, 1925 the number was 2,422, or a difference of 500. Some of these employees are girls, but at least half of the staff consists of returned men, and it is neither a simple nor an agreeable task to dispense with their services after they have served the country in the way that our returned men have done. We have made the reductions as fast as we possibly could. I am just as much impressed with the necessity of economy as is my hon. friend, and the presence or the absence of the minister in the department represents only a matter of a few thousand dollars. My hon. friend may be in the House longer than I expect, but if he is here five years from now he will rise in his place and confess that these services are absolutely necessary, unless he wishes to contend that we should stop treating those men who require treatment.

I want to make it clear
that this is not my intention in anything I have said.
Has my hon. friend (Mr. Stirling) included, in that $4,000,000 that he has given, the salaries paid to nurses and doctors?

The largest item is
$4,059,837, which appears as "salaries to staff and salaries at Ottawa."
Perhaps the minister would give us the figures for the second category.

Have you the totals?

speechtext:
I have. For the service
provided under legislation and order in council-medical treatment in the inside and outside hospitals, the amount is $4,760,585.66. That does not comprise the salaries for administration. It does comprise, of course, the [DOT]salaries of doctors, nurses, orderlies, those who *examine the patients, and so on, but not the administration. For that I have another figure.

Could the minister give
us the salaries for administration? [DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
The salaries for genera!
administration amount to $1,806,358.88, and for medical administration-not medical attendance-$368,201.16. The amount for genera! administration expenses such as telephone, telegrams, light, heat' and power, transportation and stationery is $59,941; total medical administration $428,142, or a total for administration purposes of $2,485,645.17. That is in the face of a total expenditure during 1923-24 of $51,000,000 odd. What difference would it make if, instead of placing the item for pensions in the estimates on another page, it had been placed1 under the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment on that page of the estimates we have now under our eyes? It would not make any difference at all. Only my hon. friend would be obliged to say "Oh the amount is not $10,000,000, it is $44,000,000."

Surely the minister would not contend that $34,000,000 spent for pensions is in the same category, for example, as $34,000,000 spent by the Department of Public Works, the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Railways, or any other department? Surely he would not contend that he should have anything like the proportion, or even a fraction of the proportion, of administrative costs in paying out $34,000,000 in pensions as in paying out $34,000,000 in the Department of Public Works?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I agree with my hon. friend there. I do not think the administration charges should be as large for pensions as they would be in the case that he has cited, or as they would be in the case, for instance, of a 'hospital. Still the clerical work in connection with the administration of pensions is quite large.

Has the minister the
figures for the clerical assistance in connection with the administration of pensions?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
No, I have not the figures
separated. My hon. friend knows that the two branches were merged, and the accounts division and the audit division are the same for both.
How many employees were taken into the pensions branch?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Eight hundred and eighty.

Those were taken from the
pensions branch into the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment?

Surely the minister must agree that the expense connected with the payment of these pensions has decreased since the amalgamation?

Supply-Re-establishment

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
As far as the clerical staff
is concerned I am informed dt has decreased but I doubt whether in some other respects -like the medical examination of pensioners -it has really decreased or not.

Have not the medical
boards been reduced in number in the last two or three years?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Last year we had less.
Well, I do not know exactly how many pension examinations we made a few years ago. Last year we made 40,000 such examinations. I think the number of doctors has decreased. I am not sure whether the number has decreased in the hospitals; it has decreased in the administration branch. As far as the pension examiners are concerned I am not in a position to say. Probably the number has decreased there also. The work is very difficult and very involved, and it is only by experience and by being in the position that I am to-day, that I can vouch for these statements. My hon. friends may be assured of one thing: we are not keeping one physician or one nurse that we do not require. My instructions to the officials are to keep the staff to the very lowest figure compatible with such proper discharge of the duties as the country demands. Those are the instructions and the heads of branches-the head of the medical branch and the head of the administration branch-have done all they could to reduce the staff. In very few instances have I imposed upon them the necessity of retaining someone for special meritorious reasons. They are there to testify that I have not in any way endeavoured to stop them from reducing the staff. And they have reduced it immensely; I think that has been admitted on all sides. Every one would wish that we had only 500 returned men sick and under treatment instead of three or four thousand; everyone would wish that we had less disabled returned men receiving a pension than we have. Unhappily this is a situation over which my hon. friends have no control nor have I. We have to take the situation as it is. This is a result of the war. It is deplorable that the rvar should have happened, but it has happened, and it has sent back to' this country thousands of disabled men. We have actually 44,000 disabled pensioners, and
20,000	dependent pensioners-widows mainly- in this country as a result of the war. That entails a large expenditure. No one would like to have it reduced, if that were possible, more than myself. I find no satisfaction at all in authorizing this expenditure of money nor does the House; the only satisfaction we find is in the conscientious discharge of a public
duty. I take this opportunity of saying that the department-generally speaking and in almost every respect-has been conducted above party lines. That generally speaking was true of the late administration and it has been the case with the present one. I think my hon. friends will acknowledge that I have not dismissed a great many men for political reasons in the department. Coming back to this item of capital expenditure I do not think there is any difficulty on that score. The amount spent during the year, which I said was $7,411, was only for ten months: for the complete period it is $9,000 odd.

At this late stage of the
session I do not wish to occupy very much time in dealing with any question, and I shall only speak briefly on the subject under discussion. The hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling), it appears to me, deserves the gratitude of the House, even the gratitude of the minister himself, for giving his study to these figures, for having pointed out figures which certainly look rather strange when one studies them. There is no desire on the part of the hon. member for Yale, or on the part of any member, to do other than treat the returned soldiers, the pensioners, and all the dependents of those who did not come back, with the finest type of gratitude and generosity. There is no question about that. At the same time any money which can be saved in administration and any money which can be saved in the payment of unnecessary salaries is that much less money which the people of this country generally, including the returned soldiers themselves, have to pay. In regard to the figures given by the minister, I cannot quite agree that there are $34,000,000 paid out in pensions which should be dealt with in the ordinary way, in addition to the $10,000,000 of expenditure for this department. I am now giving rather large figures, I should have said $8,500,000 paid out by this department; because certainly a large proportion of the pensions after this stage of the war would be simply repetition where you would be paying out in an ordinary routine manner pensions which are permanent. For instance, take the man who is blind, the man who has lost an arm or a leg, or any of those men with permanent injuries which are obvious- and there is quite a large proportion of them-they receive their pensions in a routine manner from year to year. The work is nothing but simply sending out cheques. So that to suggest that the spending of the $34,000,000 on pensions is in the same category as spending $34,000,000 on
Supply-R e-establishment

other lines of work would hardly be fair. I think the minister admitted to me that that was hardly on all fours. At the same time he implies that it is nearly so, and certainly it would not appear to me to be in the same category. History shows that in every country after every war new departments have been created, new staffs set up, new groups of men and women given employment, and it is difficult-I agree with the minister in that respect-to cut down the staff, and wipe out services and do away with departments, but in most countries they attempt to do it. I do not believe that in any country they ever come back after the war to the grade of expenses that existed before the war, but we should make it our endeavour, particularly with the heavy burden of taxation under which we suffer, to do our best to get back as far as we can to former conditions, because every economy that may be made is that much less money to be paid by the people generally and by the returned soldiers themselves. Without going more deeply into it, it would appear to me, looking at the figures superficially, that there is, if not too heavy, at least a very heavy proportion of the money paid out by the department in administrative expenses and salaries. I do. not say that the minister has not made an attempt to cut down some of the staff. I know that he has. Many hundreds have 'been laid off.
Last year I spoke to some of the 9 p.m. men around the country in the minister's department, and they told me that in certain branches of the department there was great overstaffing. I do not know that that is true this year, because I have not discussed the matter with them, but the salaries and administrative expenses would appear to be heavy on the face of it for the amount of money paid out,' setting aside the pensions. I can hardly agree with the minister when he makes the statement that there have been no appointments or dismissals for political purposes. I do not know that such a proceeding has been general; I doubt if it has been, but I know of at least one case, and I have heard of others. One man in Port Arthur who had served overseas, the president of the Conservative Association, was laid off, to be replaced by a Liberal who had not served overseas, for no reason except that he was of the wrong political colour. I know of other sections where the same conditions prevail. I believe that in the near future we must attempt-and this is not with any intention of criticizing the minister in that respect-to put this department in with another department. I think the
[Mr. Manion.l
time has nearly come when we should do away with that department and put it under the Department of National Defence. It would appear that we have enough administrative powers to carry on the department without loss to the soldiers and without loss to the country, and I repeat that the minister might well be advised by the hon. member for Yale, who brought up the subject, to make greater efforts than he has in the past to cut down the salaries here and there, and from an administrative standpoint to reduce expenses where it can be done without doing injury to the soldiers or their dependents.

I should like to
say a word, in regard to the general position which this department occupies. The work of the department, as I said three years ago, in the treatment of the returned soldier, will not be curtailed. I repeat-and I believe you will find it to be correct-that the number of men to be treated, while it has fallen for two or three years after the war, will begin to ascend in number. Never before did we have a war which had such far-reaching effects upon men. As far as the modern army goes, epidemics will never occur again. Scientific methods have removed the danger of an epidemic in the modern army, and if it does occur, it must only occur through the carelessness or negligence of those in charge. If you consider the effect of the late war upon the men who took part in it, by reading the papers every week you will find a record of some veteran who has suddenly passed away; some violent or sudden death will be recorded in nearly every weekly report. These are found to be due to causes of which I believe many of the medical men in charge of the treatment of returned soldiers are not aware. I have found, from constant contact with the men who served, and following them up since, that the effects of the war have not been studied by the medical men of the day as they should be. Referring to the effect on nerves, you can hardly go round any city or town where returned men are located without observing the effect of the war upon these men, and many are treating them as lead slingers, and so on, when they are really suffering from the effects of the war. Then I find that there are a great many men suffering now from the effects of gas. Bronchitis must be very frequent amongst those who were gassed, but due to lack of experience the treatment of these cases there is no great amount of sympathy in regard to them. I know that some of the expert advisers of the department can find no relation between the pulmonary troubles so frequent among those men and the

Supply-Re-establishment
effects of gas which they suffered from, but it should not be very difficult to asscertain whether a man's suffering was due to the effects of gas. It would not be very difficult to find out whether he was really on service in the zone of battle, or if 'he had served in some unit which was quite removed from that zone, in the same way as, I said some two or three years ago, you have heart cases, kidney cases and tubercular cases. These must be on the increase because they will be progressive in character, and the department, instead of turning these men down as lead slingers, as is done in many cases should sympathetically and sincerely study the case of each man. I know the minister will say:	Well, such is
done. I cannot agree with the department that it is done, because I have personal experience with many men who are affected in this way as a result of the war.
There is another class of men, of whom the. minister spoke last year, and as to whose treatment no action has been taken. That is the case of men who have aged from service. The minister knows as well as I do that there are dozens of those men who require treatment at the present time and who are not getting it. I have repeatedly requested that the government should take some action towards providing a home where these men could go for treatment. There is no use in sending them to general hospitals at the present time. The general hospital of to-day is a highly organized institution with an expert staff who will not consider that these men deserve or require that expert treatment which they should have. There are seasons of the year when this class of men will weaken, go down, and other seasons when they will, perhaps, revive and come up, and the government should provide a home where they can receive treatment as they become debilitated. These men require something in the way of particular nursing for a short time in order to bring them up again, and then they can be sent home. They are men who will never be able to do a full day's work and earn a complete livelihood, and they are not at the present time getting pension or treatment.
The great expense of this department has been brought about by unsympathetic treatment of returned men, and I am not talking now for the sake of votes or anything else from the returned men. It does not affect me whether I get that or not, but I am interested in their welfare. The government have had commission after commission. They have a pension department, a Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment and now they
have a Federal appeal board. I do not consider these were at all necessary, and I do not think the Federal appeal board amounts to a great deal as far as the men are concerned.
The returned men are not getting the benefit of government work. The Civil Service Commission, I think, are playing fair with returned men, but while government work is being carried on in different places, the returned men are not getting a fair deal in regard to it. We should remember there are many men affected by the war who cannot do a full day's work, and when government work is being carried on, these men should have the first chance.
As regards further expense, the department has made some curtailments, but it should keep in mind that where positions are available, returned men should get advantage of them. If you take up the departments one b>
one, in some cases a fairly good distribution has been made, but I think the returned men can get a little better treatment than they are getting. In 1923, in the Accounts branch there were 72 employees, 33 of whom were women. To-day there are 51 of whom 23 are women. In the Central Registry, in 1923, there were 138 employees, of whom 61 were women, and in 1924, there were 104 employees, of wnom 38 were women, two of these being married women. There are a number of these cases where the minister might explain why married women are being retained. It may be that they are widows or are selected for some particular reason, but there are a number of married women in the different branches. In the pay branch, pension division, in 1923, there were 34 employees, of whom 14 were women. Last year there were 41 employees of whom 10 were women. In the records branch, in 1923, there were 81 employees of whom 44 were women, and in 1924, there were 60 employees, of whom 20 were women, two of them being married women, and so on.
Last year I made a reference-and I think it has brought about some improvement-to the fact that a very frequent occurrence in all branches was that where employees were taken off one branch they were added to another. As a result, when reductions were made through all these branches, the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment was busy building up a very large imperial pay pension department. I pointed out that where we were paying some $34,000,000 in Canadian pensions, about 62 employees were retained, but when it came to the imperial pension pay department, paying out $7,000,-
Supply-Re-establishment

000, some 122 people were employed. That has been reduced now to 95, which I still think is a little too large. I cannot understand why 95 employees are necessary for paying out,-I think, the amount has now been increased to 810,000,000. Of these 95 employees 22 are women. As a result of the decrease in staff of these branches, we are now building up a very large Federal appeal department, the number of the employees in that department having increased to fifty. It is interesting to draw the attention of the committee to these several departments, and I think a reduction can be made. I am sympathetic with the minister in his endeavour to lead the committee and the country to believe that this department is still a very necessary one. A great work lies before the department, and I think it should undertake a general review of the whole pension field, because the men point out that to-day certain ones are receiving pensions which they never really earned, while others who were affected by active service have to fight every inch for any compensation they may receive. That is something which I think should De reviewed by medical men of the very highest professional standing in this country. I think the minister is effecting a reduction in the staff, but I am pointing out to him that those who disappear off the payroll of one department will be found on the payroll of another department the following year, and this has been complained of frequently this session.

I thank my hon. friends
from Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) and Kingston (Mr. Ross), not for their criticism that the department is not perhaps administered as it should be, but for their constructive suggestions. Last year my hon. friend from Kingston made certain suggestions which we have endeavoured to carry out. As regards the decrease in the staff, it is true the Federal appeal board was created some two years ago, and this entailed the appointment of additional employees, but the reduction of five hundred which has been effected during the past twelve or thirteen months takes in also the staff of that board. You cannot expect the process of reduction to go along faster than that. It does not make any difference whether there is a minister or not, the department or the branch, in other words, the service, will remain. Perhaps it is not absolutely necessary that a minister should be directly in charge of it, but some minister will have to have the branch under his charge and the service will have to be maintained. It is perhaps in order that 
I should say that I do not entirely share my hon. friend's view that the medical men of our service do not stand at the very head of their profession throughout Canada. In all our main cities we have in our service such men.

Will the minister
permit me to intervene? I agree with him that he has throughout the country men of the highest professional standing, but their reports are reviewed by men of lesser experience and not so prominent in their profession.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I see my hon. friend's
point. The Board of Pension Commissioners have at their disposal nine medical advisers, all men of great ability, but of course I do not know whether they stand as high in their profession as some of the medical men in Toronto, Montreal and other cities who make reports to them. But they were in the department when I took charge, and if an appointment had to be made, no minister would undertake to refuse to appoint the medical man whom the board recommended. The board is a judicial body and entitled to a certain amount of authority in the discharge of its duties. It may be that at times reports that are sent in by medical men of the highest professional standing in Vancouver, Winnipeg, Toronto, Montreal and Halifax, to headquarters, are turned down; undoubtedly in some instances this has happened, but wherever I have tried to ascertain whether this action could be laid at the door of medical officials of the board of lesser knowledge, I have failed to find that such was the case. After all, it is a matter of appreciation of the facts. In some cases, like my hon. friend from Kingston, I have thought that the reports justified the granting of pensions, and had I the same authority as the Minister of Pensions in England, I would have awarded pensions on the strength of those reports. But my judgment is not infallible, and probably the board was right. It must be remembered that out of a thousand cases you will hear a lot from one dissatisfied claimant, but you will never hear a word from the 999 satisfied pensioners. They do not complain. Why should they? My impression is that if a hundred more pensions had been awarded during the past ten years, you would not have heard any complaints. That is a small number out of the 64,000 pensions awarded, but I suppose nobody would undertake to say that those hundred cases were absolutely entitled to pensions. The board may have made some mistakes; I think they are ready to admit that they have; but who does not make mistakes? I am not here to defend the board; they are absolutely independent of me. I would never

Supply-Re-establishment
undertake to recommend to them the awarding of a pension, for it is beyond my function ; nor have I ever asked them to cancel a pension, for it is not my duty. I have in thousands of instances brought to their attention cases and asked them ito reconsider the circumstances, but without making the slightest intimation to them as to what their decision should be. Let me add that I accept with a good grace all the recommendations that have been made by my predecessor and the hon. member for Kingston, and will give them my very careful consideration.

Has the department any
information regarding two suicides which took place among the returned men in the Westminster hospital, London, Ontario? I am not prepared to say that these cases ever did occur, but I am told that one man, Garnet Ellis, who was formerly an engineer in the gaol farm, Toronto, cut his throat, as did another man, although they were both under observation at the time. Has the minister any knowledge of these cases, or has he heard anything about them?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Personally I have never
heard of any such case in the Westminster hospital, which is the main mental hospital of the department, located at London, Ontario. I am informed by the deputy minister that he does not know of any such case. It may have been an accident of which the report was somewhat exaggerated. Of course it is possible that such cases would occur among the mentally deficient.

I had a letter some time
ago from a patient in which it was stated that tubercular patients-I think it was in the Westminster hospital-were kept in the same section as drug addicts. Is there any truth in that?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
There would be drug
addicts among the mental cases in Westminster hospital, but unless they were tuberculous I do not think they would be kept in that section.

He claimed that in the
tubercular ward there were some drug addicts who were not tubercular and who were a nuisance to tubercular patients; moreover, the tubercular patients would naturally be a danger to the drug addicts. If the statement is true, the condition should be corrected. I know nothing whatever of it; I simply put it before the minister for what it is worth.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I shall make inquiry.

On May 6th, I asked the minister the following questions:
1.	Have any employees of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment been given permanent status by the minister without reference to the Civil Service Commission ?
2.	If so, what are the names and salaries of such appointees?
3.	Under what authority was such permanent status given?
In reply the minister gave a list of some twenty-four officers who had been made permanent, at salaries ranging from $4,000 to $5,000 a year. He stated also:
The Deputy Minister of Justice has advised that the minister is competent to make such appointments under para, (b) of sub-section 2, of section 5, of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment Act.
And so on. Some of these are doctors and some are not. I do not know these twenty-four men, but why should they be put on the permanent list at this stage? Moreover, the salary would appear to be higher than it should be. A man on temporary work would naturally receive more than a man whose position is permanent, but my understanding is that these men have been put on the permanent staff at the same pay that they were receiving under temporary employment. Why was that change made?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: These men are permanent not in the ordinary sense of the word but simply for the purposes of the Superannuation Act. So far as the salary is concerned, they were classified according to the rules adopted by the Civil Service Commission. In the case of those whose positions were likely to last over ten years, for instance, we found that they would be precluded from enjoying the benefits of the Superannuation Act owing to the fact that their employment was of a temporary character, and the Department of Justice gave the opinion that if the minister declared these positions permanent the officers in question could be considered by the Department of Finance as eligible to come under the Superannuation Act.

These men could be
dropped from the service at any time, by my hon. friend or any other minister, if necessary?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Yes, at any time.

Is there any likelihood of
the minister making another large group of officials permanent in the near future?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I asked the officials of
the department to make a very careful review of the staff, but as to the exact number who may come under that category I cannot say. Pensions will run over forty years, and there
Supply-Re-establishment

will be employees in the department forty years from now. Others will not be there that long; some will be employed ten, fifteen or twenty years. Some have already been there seven or eight years. It would seem to be unfair to deny them the opportunity of enjoying the provisions of the Superannuation Act.

The matter had been
drawn to my attention and I was wondering how it could be done. Personally I did not think the minister had any right to do that; however, he has the authority of the Justice department and of course I do not wish to differ from that; they know much better than I do. But at this stage it would seem that we should rather be trying to undo some positions than to make more permanent positions. I do not say this in any spirit of criticism. So far as my remarks to-night on this or any other subject are concerned I am not in any way attacking my good friend the deputy minister of the department, a gentleman with whom I have had the pleasantest relations and for whom I have the utmost respect. But I am speaking entirely from
the standpoint of economy, and it seems strange that these men should be made permanent at this time. It might be quite a lever in the hands of a minister. Of course it would not be in the hands of my hon. friend, but it would be in the hands of a minister who is not so conscientious as he is; it would give him an opportunity to make a great many men permanent just prior to an election. I should not think for a moment that the present minister would consider such a thing. But the life of the present minister is not as permanent as the jobs of some of these men who are being made so, and I would suggest to him that he defer the changing of status of these men from temporary to permanent until after the next election and let some of the rest of us attend to that for him.

Where are the tubercular
patients in New Brunswick being 'treated now? Have you given up the sanatorium at River Glade?

speechtext:
River Glade is no longer
under the department. I have mentioned only those institutions which are administered by the department directly. In River Glade we have an arrangement with the authorities for the care of patients there.

Are any patients kept in
the East St. John Tubercular hospital?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Yes, there are fourteen
in one institution and twenty-seven in the other.

The minister referred to
pay and allowance, but I see that pay and allowance is included' in the general item further down the list. What would be the differenee?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Those who are in the hos-piial for observation and special mental classification do not receive any pay and allowance.
There is a decrease in the item this year of $250,000. Is that in the nature of a reduction in the annual expenditure, or is any capital involved in it?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: There is no capital involved in it. It comprises mainly food, fuel, light, power, water rates, medical and; surgical supplies, dental equipment, laundry, maintenance of furniture and equipment, hospital and janitor supplies, patients' clothing and comforts, taxes and insurance, freight and express and other charges, and so on. There is a general reduction in food. There is a general reduction in the items I have mentioned, up to the total my hon. friend refers to.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
The cost per patient per

There certainly is a slight reduction, and there has been year after year, in the cost of food. Then there has been a reduction in outside hospitals where we have a number of patients. The statement includes equally the transportation of patients and pensioners who are called in for examination. When a soldier writes to the department and complains of a war ailment if we have no man in the vicinity, he may be

How many tubercular

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: We have only one institution for tubercular patients, and that is at Tranquille, Kamloops, where there are thirty-four patients. We have also under observation a certain number of .patients in Shaugh-nessy hospital.

In connection with the care of patients there are a number of matters I should like to draw to the minister's attention. Earlier in the session I placed a motion on the order .paper in regard to the fines imposed on patients in the hospitals of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. Since then some action has been taken in the matter, and the minister has restricted in some way the very frequent fining of patients. I should like to know what action has been taken in this regard? My point is that those who are not directly under the department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment should not have the right of imposing fines upon patients without trial.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Of course disciplinary
methods have been adopted in all hospitals. In some cases my hon. friend is of the opinion those measures have been too severely applied. The motion my hon. friend placed on the order paper had reference to these disciplinary measures, and in some instances we have thought that in order to avoid complaints on this account the superintendent of the hospital should not apply such measures without referring the case to the unit office; that in the case of the Kingston hospital, for example, the superintendent should not apply disciplinary measures without referring them for judgment to Ottawa where the head of the unit is established.

I want to draw the minister's attention to the fact that in some cases there was a regular trial, but in other
Supply-Re-establishment

units there was no trial whatever: the man was simply brought up before the superintendent or officer in charge and told "You are fined a dollar" or "You are fined a day's pay," and this, that and the other. In such cases the man had no right of appeal whatever. In the arimy a trial of the fairest character is granted1. The accused has the right to say whether his -commanding officer shall try him, or whether he shall by tried by court-martial. In any case he has the -choice of someone to defend him and the evidence is formally taken. In- many of the cases to which I aim alluding there has 'been no trial whatever. In some instances an old veteran has been fined a day's -pay, or fined an amount of something over $3, for breaking a -clinical thermometer which is never -charged up in the general hospital. In other cases a man has been fined $2 or $3 for being -twenty minutes late or staying out at night, without being given any trial or the opportunity of defending hi-msellf. I think it only needs to bring th-e matter -to the minister's attention to insure that in future such fines will not be imposed on patients without a trial being granted, the evidence recorded in writing and the accused given- some chance 'of defending himself. speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Yes, this matter has engaged the attention of the department for the last two years. As a matter of fact the parliamentary committee recommended that the establishment of soldiers' homes should engage our attention to provide for those soldiers for whom treatment cannot be of any further benefit, as my hon. friend has said. It is difficult to say what the exact number of these men would be, but in order to meet the situation we have thought we should reserve in some of the hospitals a ward to provide them as an asylum. The department would house, feed and clothe the men, and in most cases they would make their own bed and in other ways attend to themselves. Usually their ward disability is small, but other disabilities prevent them from taking up work of any kind. With that in view, we have adopted an order in council, a copy of which I shall be glad to send to my hon. friend at any time, but he can find it on page 46 of the departmental report. It sets
out the conditions under which these patients may avail themselves of this opportunity. So far, I am informed by the director of medical services, we have only seven patients Who have been transferred from active treatment to another ward where they do not receive pay and allowances. We started this system two months ago and we are making the selection very carefully. The director of medical services has instructions to review all the hospitals and try to segregate these cases. In the ordinary course these men should be discharged from hospital, but occasionally it is almost impossible to do so, for it would mean putting them on the street. We offer them the option of remaining in the hospital without pay and allowances, they receiving the pensions that the board awards to them. If the pension is large enough we retain a certain amount for their maintenance. I fancy this scheme will be a great relief to such men, for their families are relieved of the obligation of maintaining them, and having become accustomed to the hospital the men find themselves more or less at home. Undoubtedly they will in large numbers avail themselves of this opportunity, and I think the saving in expense will be considerable, as my hon. friend has pointed out.

It seems to me that the

expectation of life diminishes more claims will have to be paid, and it is not in my power to say what will be the outcome. It is possible that in the future the government will have to lay out some money in this connection.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I listened with interest
to the resolution quoted by the hon. gentleman, and I may assure him that as a matter of fact the DeSouttar limb has been engaging the attention of the department for the last two or three years. Personally I have been much interested in it; but whatever may be said in favour of it, even in England it is still in the experimental stage. The British Ministry of Pensions has not adopted the DeSouttar limb definitely. We have purchased a few of these limbs in order to carry on our observations. It is not a question of dollars and cents, and if the DeSouttar limb will benefit the amputation cases to a greater extent than the limb we manufacture here, we are willing to pay the extra cost; there is a difference, I think, of about $70 each in the cost of the two limbs. The DeSouttar limb is somewhat lighter; I am informed it is eight to ten ounces lighter than the limb our men wear. I am also informed that a number of amputation cases like the DeSouttar limb. On the other hand others have said to me that they prefer the Canadian limb. Whether or not we should say to the amputation cases "You are welcome to the DeSouttar limlb if you want it" is a matter for consideration and discussion. So far we have not decided to do that. There are other

Supply-Re-establishment

limbs available. It has been represented to me that there are metal limbs that are just as good as the DeSouttar limb. The latter is an expensive appliance; I think it is covered by patent although I am not sure, and it would be costly to make the change. Before we do so we ought to be absolutely secure in our position that the change is warranted by the superior qualities of the DeSouttar limb. That limb is still in the experimental stage, and we need further evidence before reaching a final decision in the matter. There is now in the city a representative of the British Ministry of Pensions. This gentleman arrived in Canada lately, but unfortunately I have not had an opportunity of conversing with him as yet. It was arranged that he should see me this afternoon, but I was detained in the House on account of the possibility of my estimates coming up at any moment. However, I intend to discuss the question further with this representative of the British Ministry of Pensions. In the meantime if my hon. friend (Mr. Black, Yukon) will send me a copy of the resolution which he read I will attach it to imy file and it may prove to be useful.

The DeSouttar limb has been in use to my knowledge since 1918, and may have been used before that year, but if so only to a very limited extent. I cannot help thinking that the letter read by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black) is perhaps unduly favourable to the DeSouttar limb. It is a good limb and particularly suitable in certain cases. On the other hand in some cases there is a disadvantage in having a light limb. It is not true that the lighter the limb the better it is. There is a certain weight of limb which is more suitable than others to some men. In the case of a light limb, if there is a strong wind there is a tendency that the limb will be blown from underneath the user. However I do not wish to disparage the DeSouttar limb; it is a very fine limb in certain cases. I do not think one would go the length of saying that this limb should be supplied in all instances because it is not necessarily the most suitable or the best. The British government has not made general use of the DeSouttar limb, one reason being that the expense rendered that impossible. Furthermore, as I say, in certain cases the DeSouttar limb is not especially suitable. I believe there has been some arrangement made whereby, if an amputation case desires the DeSouttar limib the cost of an ordinary limb is allowed towards its purchase. As regards the artificial limbs that are made [Mr. B41and.)
in Canada by the department, it is only fair to say-and I make the statement from personal knowledge-they are,-shall I say, in the cases that have come to my notice-highly satisfactory. I am aware of cases where the men, in tlhe hope of obtaining a better limb, or the best limb procurable, have gone to a large centre like New York, but have finally returned home convinced that a more serviceable limb is supplied by the department over which the minister presides than can be obtained elsewhere. As regards the ordinary limb, in many cases the make is very superior and very satisfactory. I think it is only fair to acknowledge the good work that is being done here in that respect. I believe that as time goes on we may be able to secure a still better limb. I believe there is a combination between the metal and the wocden limb which possesses many advantages and can be had for a reasonable price.

I am astonished
to hear any hon. member suggest that if an amputation case requires this better type of artificial limb the government should advance him the price of an ordinary wooden leg, and that he should pay the balance. That is a policy that is altogether too economical.

May I correct the hon.
member. I,stated that I was under the impression that the British government had arranged that plan. I did not advocate it- or express an opinion about it.

I think my correspondent stated the case in the most convincing way when he said that the only authority on the subject is the man who has to wear the artificial limib. I am very glad indeed that my hon. friend (Mr. MacLaren) has never been in that position. I quoted to the House the opinion of a man who has to wear a wooden leg. I happen to have known this man for some twenty years past, and by the way he comes from my hon. friend's constituency St. John and lived there until he moved west. He was a big strapping fellow, but now is a helpless cripple having lost his leg above the knee while on active service in France. I have another letter from the Dominion secretary-treasurer of the Amputation Association of the Great war in which he says:
The DeSouttar leg is quite popular on the other side, and a great number of them are being issued to the men. We have been trying to get a number of them sent out to this country, but the DeSouttar people refuse to ship a lesser quantity than one hundred, so we understand, and the department will not consider this.

Supply-Re-establishment
So, apparently, the matter of expense is a big factor in determining this question. I submit that the question of expense should not be considered for a moment in equipping Canada's lame returned men with the best artificial limb that can be found.

speechtext: No.

speechtext: We will reserve that.
If the minister will answer a question or two, I would appreciate it. For instance, what is the item $5,000 for special publicity?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Advertising in the veteran papers about the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment and about the delays and when they expire for presenting claims for pensions, and all other claims-all the veteran papers.

What papers are
they?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
The Khaki Call, The Listening Post, Imperial Veteran, Manitoba Veteran, The Veteran, Canadian Review Company Limited, Labour Leader. This is a very reduced service now.
Supply-Re-establishment
What is the operating expense?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
The largest amount of the operating expense item is used to provide advances for treatment of imperial pensioners and allied country pensioners who are in Canada, we being the agent of the governments concerned. A large amount of this money that is provided is being reimbursed to the department. The other portion is used generally for:
Telephone, telegrams, postage and car fare.
Transportation and travelling of staff.
Stationery and office supplies.
Insurance and storage.
Light, heat, power and water rates.
Maintenance and repairs to furniture and equipment.
Freight and express.
Royal Commission on Pensions and Re-Establishment.
Other general expenses.
Working capital.
Financing treatment and medical examination of imperial and foreign former soldiers; also miscellaneous expense of Imperial pension office.
All of this is refunded, but it is refunded month by month, and we are generally a large amount behind. We have to provide the money. The main sum in this connection is spent on behalf of Imperial government.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I am afraid they will come up late in the session, and you will not have the same opportunity that you would have to-night. I know that the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Ross) wants to ask a few questions regarding quarantine.
If the minister is so interested in getting this item through, I think we will have to go back and discuss some of the items we have carried.

While the minister is satisfied, the rest of us would like to proceed with some of the business of the House, if that is possible.

The arrangement was to go on with the Health estimates. It was the Health estimates I was interested in.
The minister may take up any item he likes, but he will not get any of them through.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I do not think my hon. friend means that. He enjoys a good reputation in the House and he must not destroy it.
I am not afraid of that. I think my hon. friend is not fair. We made the arrangement and now he comes forward with a proposition to pass the Health estimates. That matter was not discussed.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Oh yes.
We had an understanding.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I said I would be perfectly willing to reserve one or two items, take the Health items which remain to be adopted and adopt them this evening after proper discussion, and I pointed out in this connection that the Health estimates have already been under consideration quite a long time in the House, and a tremendous amount of information has been supplied to the committee and properly so. The remaining Health department items are not nearly as important as those we have adopted. The only three items left include one very small amount, the quarantine item which we discussed very extensively the other day, but regarding which seme information could still be supplied, and the other one is venereal diseases, which is a grant.

We have been getting along very nicely, and rather than disturb the House at this time, I think the minister would be well advised, if the arrangement was entered into, to let the. House adjourn at eleven o'clock. We have put through estimates totalling nearly $8,000,000 to-night, and although I would like to see the Health estimates get through to-night, there is one item, venereal diseases, that might involve a general discussion.
